sections.overview: The black slug is a very large land slug of north-western Europe. The name covers a complex of close relatives that can only be told apart reliably by dissection or DNA, so records are often made for the group as a whole. It is a nocturnal omnivore that favours moist, vegetated ground.
sections.identification: Adults measure about 75–180 mm in one source and 90–140 mm in another. The body is bulky, with long coarse tubercles along the back and sides and no keel, and it contracts into a bell shape. Colour varies from black to brown, grey, green, orange or red, and a jet-black form lives on peatlands. Young slugs are pale yellow to orange and darken with age. Reliable adult body-mass and sex-specific size figures were not found in the consulted sources.
sections.habitat: It is found in farmland, hedge bottoms, woodland, wetland margins and peatland, up to moderate altitudes, and is common in any well-vegetated area. Sources disagree on gardens: one calls it common there, another rare there because of competition from other slugs. Its exact world range is uncertain because of the identification problem.
sections.diet: It is omnivorous, eating carrion, dung, fungi and plants, with occasional worms and insects. It prefers rotting vegetation to living plants, so it often does little harm in gardens, although it can damage crops. It feeds mostly at night with a rasping tongue, the radula.
sections.behavior: It is largely nocturnal and most easily found after rain or at night, from spring to autumn, and needs moist surfaces to move. Large numbers can gather on freshly mown verges after daytime rain. When irritated it contracts and rocks strongly from side to side.
sections.reproduction: The slug is hermaphroditic. One source says it cross-fertilises when a mate is available and lays 20–50 eggs in soil crevices or decaying wood, hatching in about six weeks, while an Irish source says reproduction is mainly by self-fertilisation, with copulation rarely seen. The eggs are pearly white and about 5 mm across, often found in compost heaps.
sections.ecology: By eating dead plant matter, carrion and dung, the black slug recycles nutrients back into the soil. In towns it becomes less frequent, apparently through competition with other slug species.
sections.conservation: The Irish mollusc survey lists Arion ater ater as Least Concern, and it is described as extremely common and widespread in Britain. Animal Diversity Web lists no special conservation status; these are not a global assessment of the whole species complex.
